action_prescription.common_failure: The common failure is not lack of knowledge. It is remembering the tool only after the emotion is already high.
action_prescription.do_not_overread: Treat “Empathy with a Boundary” as low-risk self-observation and communication preparation, not therapy, crisis support, a guarantee of relationship repair, or advice for unsafe, coercive, abusive, trauma-triggering, or clearly power-imbalanced situations. If safety, ongoing distress, or high-conflict dynamics are involved, prioritize trusted support or professional help.
action_prescription.do_today: Today, use one low-risk version of this sentence: “I can see this is heavy for you. I can help you sort the next step, but I cannot carry the whole weight for you.”
action_prescription.repair_move: If you miss it, do not restart the whole plan. Review one trigger and one first sentence for next time.
action_prescription.script: I can see this is heavy for you. I can help you sort the next step, but I cannot carry the whole weight for you.

seven_day_plan.practice: List one recent moment when you carried someone else’s load.
Commit to only one specific support action.
Notice your body after stating a boundary.
Review whether the boundary actually harmed the relationship.
Choose one situation next week where you will not automatically take over.

action_prescription.title: Empathy with a Boundary
action_prescription.watch_out: Do not treat this practice as a demand to change yourself or another person immediately. Use it only in low-risk, exit-safe situations without clear coercion or power pressure, and look for one clearer pause, sentence, or review.
action_prescription.why_this_matters: After understanding someone, clarify what you can support and what you cannot carry for them.

core_formulation.core_claim: The issue is not “too much empathy.” The leverage point is separating understanding, responsibility, action, and recovery. Power dynamics, closeness, and stress level can change how this pattern shows up.
core_formulation.development_lever: Practice a post-empathy boundary sentence: name the feeling, then state what you can and cannot take on.
core_formulation.do_not_overread: Check this interpretation against real feedback and specific situations; it does not replace behavioral observation.
evidence_basis: The four relative dimension positions and response quality support this interpretation; check it against real situations.
core_formulation.likely_cost: Without a clear boundary, “I understand” can slide into “I have to carry this.”
core_formulation.one_liner: In this self-report, you appear quick to notice emotional cues in others, while recovery after emotionally loaded contact may take more space.
core_formulation.primary_strength: You may be quick to notice what someone is feeling before they state it directly, and you may use understanding to maintain connection.
core_formulation.share_line: This self-report suggests you often notice others’ emotions and may need clearer recovery and boundaries afterward.
core_formulation.title: Self-reported pattern: Strong empathy cues, heavier recovery load

boundary.claim_boundary: Not for emotional-ability ranking, career prediction, hiring, clinical diagnosis, relationship-outcome judgment, fixed identity labels, or high-stakes decisions.
boundary.how_to_use: Treat MBTI, Big Five, Enneagram, RIASEC, and related results as reflection signals from different question frameworks. They can help form better questions, but they do not rewrite EQ scores, replace EQ-60 self-report, or prove real-world behavior.
boundary.summary: This module only explains how related assessments can support reading the EQ-60 result. It does not combine multiple tests into a more “true” conclusion.
boundary.title: Cross-Assessment Context Boundary

mechanisms.cost: The cost is that clearer signals can create more pressure or self-criticism when follow-through is weaker.
mechanisms.development_lever: Next practice focus: Translate understanding into one small move: acknowledge, ask, or offer options without deciding for them. Use it as a concrete review entry point, not proof of a fixed deficit.
mechanisms.do_not_overread: Check understanding another person and choosing a relational response in a real situation; the EM_RM score combination does not establish cause or ability.
mechanisms.micro_action: Micro-action: in the next similar scene, add only one step. Translate understanding into one small move: acknowledge, ask, or offer options without deciding for them.
mechanisms.strength: The strength is a clear entry point: you know where the chain begins.
mechanisms.title: Empathy understanding x relationship management: strong cue, weaker follow-through
mechanisms.what_it_feels_like: The first signal is clearer, but the second step may be less steady, creating a “noticed it but could not carry it forward” pattern.
mechanisms.why_it_matters: This mechanism focuses on how emotional cues you notice become visible and appropriate relational action. It helps locate which link in the chain needs observation, but it cannot by itself predict real-world behavior.

mechanisms.cost: The cost is that action may bypass important feeling data and require later review.
mechanisms.development_lever: Next practice focus: Separate “what I feel” and “what I notice in the other person” into two sentences. Use it as a concrete review entry point, not proof of a fixed deficit.
mechanisms.do_not_overread: Check separating your feelings from the other person’s feelings in a real situation; the SA_EM score combination does not establish cause or ability.
mechanisms.micro_action: Micro-action: in the next similar scene, add only one step. Separate “what I feel” and “what I notice in the other person” into two sentences.
mechanisms.strength: The strength is having an executable move rather than getting fully stuck.
mechanisms.title: Self-awareness x empathy understanding: steadier action, less clear source
mechanisms.what_it_feels_like: The second step feels more available than the first, so action may happen before the emotional source is fully understood.
mechanisms.why_it_matters: This mechanism focuses on how you distinguish your own feelings from the other person’s feelings. It helps locate which link in the chain needs observation, but it cannot by itself predict real-world behavior.

psychometric_evidence_status.body: Current standard scores, percentiles, and bands use a provisional norming approach. They describe relative self-report position in the current sample and version, not final global norms, ability ranking, or real-world performance ranking.
psychometric_evidence_status.do_not_overread: Percentiles are relative positions in the current versioned provisional sample.
psychometric_evidence_status.next_validation_step: Continue expanding samples, stratify by language/region/age and related variables, and publish norm-version notes with interpretation limits.
psychometric_evidence_status.what_this_means_for_user: Scores can help locate this response pattern roughly within the current sample, but should not be used to compare personal worth, ability level, career prospects, or relationship quality.

psychometric_evidence_status.body: EQ-60 items, the four-dimension structure, and result-page interpretations have been mapped to self-reported emotional and relational functioning. The current evidence mainly supports content coverage and interpretation boundaries, not formal criterion validation or ability measurement.
psychometric_evidence_status.do_not_overread: Current evidence supports content coverage and interpretation boundaries only.
psychometric_evidence_status.next_validation_step: Continue review by psychometric, boundary, and localization reviewers for item coverage, dimension assignment, cultural context, and misinterpretation risk.
psychometric_evidence_status.what_this_means_for_user: Use the report as a structured self-reflection tool for organizing self-perceived signals in awareness, regulation, empathy, and relationship management.

psychometric_evidence_status.body: Internal consistency should be estimated by language, region, and dimension after sufficient sample accumulation, with version tracking for item and report changes. The current page should not imply completed reliability evidence.
psychometric_evidence_status.do_not_overread: Internal-consistency evidence still needs accumulation by language and dimension.
psychometric_evidence_status.next_validation_step: After sample growth, report alpha/omega or more suitable reliability indices by dimension and inspect the effect of low-quality responses on estimates.
psychometric_evidence_status.what_this_means_for_user: Dimension scores can help read this response pattern, but should not be treated as fully reliability-validated stable measures.

psychometric_evidence_status.body: The four-dimension model currently serves as the report interpretation framework. Suitable exploratory/confirmatory analyses are still needed to test whether items consistently support SA, ER, EM, and RM.
psychometric_evidence_status.do_not_overread: The four-dimension structure still needs testing in larger samples.
psychometric_evidence_status.next_validation_step: Use larger samples to examine EFA/CFA results, item loadings, dimension correlations, and model fit, with separate checks by language version.
psychometric_evidence_status.what_this_means_for_user: The four-quadrant matrix is useful for organizing the report, but should not be read as a fully cross-sample-validated final factor model.

psychometric_evidence_status.body: Test-retest stability still needs observation over appropriate time windows. EQ-60 is self-report, so recent stress, relationship events, and response state may influence results.
psychometric_evidence_status.do_not_overread: Compare trends after 30–90 days or a meaningful life change.
psychometric_evidence_status.next_validation_step: Compare retests over reasonable windows such as 30–90 days to separate stable self-perception, situational fluctuation, and low-quality response effects.
psychometric_evidence_status.what_this_means_for_user: If your recent circumstances have shifted substantially, read this result as a current self-report snapshot rather than a permanent label.

psychometric_evidence_status.body: Measurement invariance across Chinese/English versions, regions, and user groups still needs testing. Without invariance evidence, score meanings should not be directly compared across languages or groups.
psychometric_evidence_status.do_not_overread: Scores should not be directly compared across languages or groups.
psychometric_evidence_status.next_validation_step: Check DIF, item interpretation differences, dimension structure, and score distributions by language and major user group; adjust interpretation where needed rather than forcing equivalence.
psychometric_evidence_status.what_this_means_for_user: Both Chinese and English reports can support localized self-reflection, but percentile differences across languages, cultures, or groups should not be read as ability differences.

psychometric_evidence_status.body: External-association evidence is not being used to support high-stakes decisions. Future work may only explore links with low-risk indicators such as self-reported recovery, communication satisfaction, or growth-goal completion.
psychometric_evidence_status.do_not_overread: Current results cannot predict relationship, work, or health outcomes.
psychometric_evidence_status.next_validation_step: Design low-risk, non-hiring, non-clinical external-indicator studies and state clearly that association is not prediction or causation.
psychometric_evidence_status.what_this_means_for_user: The result does not prove job performance, relationship outcomes, mental-health status, or career success. It is a reference for self-understanding and low-risk action planning.

quality_confidence.body: Your response pace and consistency support normal report reading.
quality_confidence.how_to_read: Start with the key finding and supporting scores, then compare the selected scenes with your recent experience.
quality_confidence.label: High interpretation confidence
quality_confidence.retest_note: If you want to observe change, retest after 30–90 days or after a meaningful life change.
quality_confidence.user_guidance: You can read the core pattern, dimension summary, and action suggestions while keeping them as self-report interpretation, not ability ranking or external evaluation.
quality_confidence.what_to_hold_lightly: Specific scores, percentiles, and bands are still estimates within a provisional sample; they are not precise ability rankings, diagnoses, or career judgments.
quality_confidence.what_to_trust: The relative dimension pattern, selected interpretation, and selected scenes can be read with normal confidence.
quality_confidence.why_this_level: Speed, repeated choices, extreme/neutral responding, and consistency signals did not show a clear response-quality risk.

reality_scenes.better_move: Do one thing: rewrite the current difficulty as roles, one owner, and a deadline.
reality_scenes.context: When several people work with unclear goals, overlapping responsibility, or uneven pace.
reality_scenes.cost: When roles are unclear, the person most willing to coordinate can inherit unnamed responsibility.
reality_scenes.do_not_overread: This is a teamwork observation, not a judgment of anyone's ability.
reality_scenes.micro_script: Who owns this, when is it due, and who decides if it gets blocked?
reality_scenes.reflection_prompt: Record the owner, deadline, and who decides when work is blocked.
reality_scenes.reflection_question: Are you completing your role, or carrying coordination work the team has not named?
reality_scenes.result_page_depth: For teamwork review, not for judging team or individual performance.
reality_scenes.strength: The useful possibility is noticing task and relationship demands together, then making hidden work explicit.
reality_scenes.tiny_experiment: Before the next collaboration, record the owner, decision maker, and deadline.
reality_scenes.title: Team collaboration: translate atmosphere into roles
reality_scenes.typical_response: This response suggests the self-perceived pattern “Strong empathy cues, heavier recovery load.” In teamwork, check whether you quietly take on emotional coordination or gap-filling beyond the task itself.
reality_scenes.why_this_matters: Converts team atmosphere into roles and process that can be checked.

reality_scenes.better_move: Do one thing: schedule a defined short pause before explaining, committing, or deciding.
reality_scenes.context: After sustained demand, urgency, or emotional load, when communication or a decision is still required.
reality_scenes.cost: Without recovery, regulation can become suppression and later appear as numbness, escalation, or avoidance.
reality_scenes.do_not_overread: Persistent sleep loss, severe distress, or impaired functioning needs real-world support, not only a micro-practice.
reality_scenes.micro_script: I need ten minutes to recover my attention, then I can give you a clear response.
reality_scenes.reflection_prompt: Record the pressure cue, pause length, and response after recovery.
reality_scenes.reflection_question: Can you still understand the information and decide, or are you only sustaining a reaction?
reality_scenes.result_page_depth: For recovery-rhythm review, not for clinical or functioning judgments.
reality_scenes.strength: The useful possibility is treating fatigue as a state that needs care, not as a character flaw.
reality_scenes.tiny_experiment: At the next pressure spike, take one short pause and then note whether the decision became clearer.
reality_scenes.title: Pressure recovery: recover before committing
reality_scenes.typical_response: This response suggests the self-perceived pattern “Strong empathy cues, heavier recovery load.” As pressure accumulates, check whether you notice reduced attention instead of treating endurance as steadiness.
reality_scenes.why_this_matters: Turns endurance into one explicit, schedulable recovery step.

reality_scenes.better_move: Do one thing: verify whether people can pause, ask for help, or hand off work as pressure rises.
reality_scenes.context: When checking team norms, management style, feedback rhythm, interpersonal density, and recovery space.
reality_scenes.cost: Treating environment preferences as job fit can miss actual duties, culture, management, and life stage.
reality_scenes.do_not_overread: These are conditions to verify, not evidence of job fit, selection, or performance.
reality_scenes.micro_script: When pressure rises here, can people pause, ask for help, or hand work off?
reality_scenes.reflection_prompt: Record one real environment, observable evidence, and one open question.
reality_scenes.reflection_question: Is feedback specific, can conflict pause, are boundaries respected, and can recovery be planned?
reality_scenes.result_page_depth: For checking work conditions, not for job-fit or performance prediction.
reality_scenes.strength: The useful possibility is turning an abstract result into questions for a real team or role.
reality_scenes.tiny_experiment: Choose one real team and answer this environment question from public rules or direct experience.
reality_scenes.title: Work-environment conditions to verify
reality_scenes.typical_response: This response suggests the self-perceived pattern “Strong empathy cues, heavier recovery load.” It cannot decide which role fits; it only points to work conditions worth checking for communication load, boundaries, and recovery.
reality_scenes.why_this_matters: Replaces a career judgment with a check of actual work conditions.

bullets: practice separating understanding someone from carrying the situation for them.

EM.what_low_can_look_like: You may focus on tasks or facts and miss some emotional cues.

ER.definition: A self-reported tendency to pause, reset, and choose responses after pressure, feedback, frustration, or conflict; it is not the same as always staying calm, suppressing emotion, or proving resilience.

ER.what_low_can_look_like: Recovery may take longer after being triggered, with avoidance, over-explaining, or suppression becoming common.

RM.what_low_can_look_like: Even when feelings are clear, repairing or moving the conversation forward may be harder.

SA.what_low_can_look_like: Feelings may become clear only afterward, making it easier to react before understanding.

This assessment is a self‑report questionnaire for self‑reflection and skill development. It is not a medical diagnosis or psychotherapy advice.

free_blocks.content: Response quality is **A**: consistency and pacing are stable; interpretability is high.
free_blocks.title: Response Quality

free_blocks.content:
Your overall EQ standard score is **99.5** (population mean 100, SD 15), at the **48.67** percentile.

This assessment covers four capabilities: Self‑Awareness (SA), Emotion Regulation (ER), Social Awareness & Empathy (EM), and Relationship Management (RM). Each section includes a standard score and a maturity band to locate strengths and training priorities.

Response quality: **A**.
free_blocks.title: Overview

free_blocks.content:
**Dimension: Self‑Awareness**

Standard score: **97** (42.07 percentile), band: **Competent**.

You usually identify emotions and connect them to triggers and needs. In many situations you can say things like “I’m tense,” “I need a moment,” or “I felt overlooked.” This reduces misunderstanding and rumination, keeping conversations closer to the real issue.

**Practice**: Before a key conversation, write one sentence: “What matters most to me here?”
free_blocks.title: Self‑Awareness · Competent

free_blocks.content:
**Dimension: Emotion Regulation**

Standard score: **83** (12.85 percentile), band: **Baseline**.

Under pressure or triggers, emotions can take over the action system—impulses, rumination, sleep disruption, or prolonged tension. This is not a “willpower” label; it reflects a toolbox that isn’t automatic yet. Regulation aims to bring intensity and duration back into a manageable range, not to erase emotions.

**90‑second reset**: Pause → slow exhale 6 times → feel your feet on the ground to create space before reacting.
free_blocks.title: Emotion Regulation · Baseline

free_blocks.content:
**Dimension: Social Awareness & Empathy**

Standard score: **119** (89.74 percentile), band: **Exceptional**.

Your empathy is exceptionally strong. Even in noisy environments you read emotions and motives accurately and respond with warmth. This is a foundation of influence. Keep boundaries to prevent emotional overload.

**Practice**: Use: “I see this is hard for you. I can stay with you for a bit,” while keeping your limits.
free_blocks.title: Social Awareness & Empathy · Exceptional

free_blocks.content:
**Dimension: Relationship Management**

Standard score: **99** (47.34 percentile), band: **Competent**.

You communicate and collaborate well, maintain trust, and manage disagreements without breaking the relationship. You tend to balance authenticity with relationship care.

**Practice**: In conflict, align on the shared goal first, then discuss options.
free_blocks.title: Relationship Management · Competent

free_blocks.content:
**Primary profile: Compassion Overload (High Empathy + Low Regulation)**

Your results show Empathy **119** very high and Emotion Regulation **83** lower. You feel others’ pain and stress strongly, and group climate can affect you quickly. The gift is warmth and attunement; the cost is overload and blurry boundaries.

**Typical strengths**
- High resonance: people open up to you easily.
- Strong ‘room reading’: you sense shifts and hidden tension.
- Care motive: a real drive to help.

**Typical costs**
- Emotional contagion: others’ feelings enter your body and drain sleep/energy.
- Rescue reflex: urgency to fix, leading to over‑involvement.
- Boundary loss: ‘empathy’ turns into ‘carrying,’ then burnout.

**Key shift: bounded care**
High empathy doesn’t require self‑sacrifice. Training focuses on three boundaries:
1) **Emotional boundary**: “This is theirs” vs “this is mine.”
2) **Time boundary**: define how long you can be available.
3) **Action boundary**: move from ‘fixing’ to ‘helping them see choices.’

**Support scripts**
- “I hear this is hard. I can stay with you for 10 minutes to sort it out.”
- “What I can offer is … The deeper choice is yours.”
- “I care about you, and I also need to protect my energy.”

**What this free report gives you**
- Boundary training to turn empathy into a resource.
- Regulation tools to prevent overload spillover.
- 14‑day plan for sustainable helping.
free_blocks.title: Compassion Overload

free_blocks.content:
**14‑Day Plan: Boundaried Care (10–15 min/day)**

Goal: keep your warmth and sensitivity while building emotional, time, and action boundaries to prevent overload.

| Day | Theme | Practice |
|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Mine vs yours | Note one contagion moment: whose emotion is it? what can I do? |
| Day 2 | Emotional boundary | Practice: “I see it’s hard for you. This is your feeling. I’m here with you.” |
| Day 3 | Time boundary | Set a time cap (10/20 min) and write an ending script. |
| Day 4 | Action boundary | Shift from fixing to options: write 3 guiding questions. |
| Day 5 | Back to body | 2‑minute tactile grounding (cup/table texture). |
| Day 6 | Self‑compassion | Write 3 lines: this is hard; I’m not alone; I’ll be kind to myself. |
| Day 7 | Support & referral | List 3 resources you can hand off to; don’t carry alone. |
| Day 8 | Empathize without spiraling | Reflect feeling, then ask: listen or brainstorm? |
| Day 9 | Energy return | After deep listening: 5 minutes walk/breath to reset. |
| Day10 | State limits | Use: “I can stay up to here; then I need rest.” once. |
| Day11 | Load monitoring | Rate emotional load 0–10; above 7, reduce inputs intentionally. |
| Day12 | One smallest act | Keep helping action to 1 minimal step; avoid over‑involvement. |
| Day13 | Relationship structure | Pick one draining relationship: what boundary makes it sustainable? |
| Day14 | Consolidate | 3 boundary principles + 3 care scripts. |

Boundaries aren’t coldness—they make care sustainable.
free_blocks.title: Boundaried Care

free_blocks.content:
**Scoring (Production v1.0)**

1) 60 items use a 5‑point scale; reverse‑keyed items are flipped before aggregation (6 − response).
2) Each quadrant has 15 items. Raw sums are mapped to standard scores (mean 100, SD 15).
3) Response‑quality indicators are computed (time, long‑stringing, extreme/neutral bias, internal consistency). Only A/B quality enters the norm pool.
4) This free report includes cross‑quadrant insights and a 14‑day training plan to convert understanding into practice.
free_blocks.title: Methodology

free_blocks.content:
**How to use this report**: Treat this as guidance for self‑reflection and skill training. A retake interval of at least 14 days improves stability.
This platform does not use a single test result for labeling decisions.
free_blocks.title: Closing Notes
